catalog_quote: A small number of words have no accented syllable of their own (certain conjunctions, most prepositions and the word ne 'not' before a verb are proclitics ...). Apart from these, every word form has one accented syllable (some compound words have one on each element). We say accent, not stress, because pitch and length are involved rather than intensity. Accent can alternate in placement or contour within the paradigm of a word. Accented syllables are termed either rising or falling, and contain a long or a short vowel. Traditional notation in grammars and dictionaries combines these two features, using four accent marks: short falling \\ as in ȁ, long falling ⌒ as in ȃ, short rising \ as in à, long rising ⁄ as in á. The falling accents occur almost exclusively on first syllables of words, and can occur on monosyllables: gȍvōr 'speech', lȍš 'bad'; prȃvdati 'to justify', grȃd 'city'. The…
sweep_summary: 18 title hits for Serbian-Croatian-Bosnian (catalog: tonal, per Browne & Alt 2004). Read in full: Arsenijević & Simonović 2013 (lingbuzz preprint), Simonović & Kager 2023 (CC BY published form of the 2017 'From accent to stress' talk, via the Internet Archive), Diesing & Zec 2017 (Glossa, via the Internet Archive), Yu 2008 (UCLA MA, via the Internet Archive), plus two hrcak articles on Klaić 2013 (Opačić 2014, Vidović 2014) and the on-disk Zsiga & Zec 2013 / Zec & Zsiga 2010 / Landau et al. 1995. All first-hand statements agree with the catalog for the codified Neo-Štokavian standard: one contrastive lexical H (four traditional accents = tone x length), stress predictable from tone (initial, or the syllable before a non-initial H), falling accents only word-initial, no final accent in native words, monosyllables only falling. New refinement: Simonović & Kager 2023 document that the de facto standard in Zagreb, Rijeka, Pula, Niš etc. is a stress-only system without tone or length (contrastive stress in nouns, predictable stem-final stress in verbs); Yu 2008 independently notes Zagreb speakers neutralise the pitch accent contrast. Not obtainable: Werle 2009 dissertation (ScholarWorks 403; high priority as the fullest generative overview), Bidwell 1968 / Lehfeldt 1970 / Peukert 1969 / Babić 1988 (De Gruyter paywall), Lehiste & Ivić 1982 (Benjamins), Inkelas & Zec 1988 (abstract only), Simonović & Arsenijević 2015 x2 (academia.edu 403), Alexander 2008 and Radanović-Kocić 1996 (print, clitic placement, not word stress), Klaić 2013 (book; medium priority, described by its reviewers as the most complete Croatian accent handbook). searches were done by direct downloads, Crossref/DataCite APIs and the the Internet Archive.

new_statements.quote: Standard Serbo-Croatian has two groups of varieties that differ in prosody. On the one hand, there are pitch-accent varieties with contrastive vowel length, spoken in what is traditionally considered the Neo-Štokavian dialect area (e.g., in Osijek, Zadar, Split, Novi Sad and Belgrade). On the other hand, there are stress varieties without contrastive vowel length, spoken in cities in what are traditionally considered Old-Štokavian and Non-Štokavian dialect areas (e.g., in Zagreb, Rijeka, Pula, Niš, Zaječar and Bor). [...] In stress standard SC the stress position in verbs is predictable [...] verbal stress in stress standard SC is typically stem-final.

new_statements.reading: Two coexisting implementations of the standard: (a) the codified Neo-Štokavian pitch accent standard, in which a lexical high tone plus length is contrastive and stress is derived from tone (initial, or the syllable before a non-initial H; never final) — this is what the catalog codes as 'tonal' and what Zsiga & Zec 2013 (also read: 'stress falls on the syllable that immediately precedes the one specified for tone, if there is one, otherwise on the initial syllable.. stress cannot fall on the final syllable of polysyllables') describe; and (b) the urban 'stress standard' (Zagreb, Rijeka, Pula, Niš, Bor, Zaječar), a pure lexical-stress system with no tone or length, contrastive stress in nouns (ˈnovine vs noˈvine) and predictable stem-final stress in verbs. So the catalog's 'tonal' coding is correct for the codified standard but this search of works with stress in the title documents a large stress-only variety of the same language that a lexical-stress catalog should note.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog's classification of the codified standard as tonal/pitch accent (High Tone plus stress; stress derived from tone) and with the Zsiga & Zec statement already held by the project; contributes no placement rule and nothing about the urban stress-only varieties.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Schütze treats Serbo-Croatian word prosody as a lexical High Tone (pitch accent) plus stress system, following Inkelas & Zec 1988 / Zec 1993: every prosodic word surfaces with a High Tone and stress (toneless words get a default High Tone), and tone spreading rules operate within words and, in some dialects, from a word onto a preceding preposition. He gives no rule for where stress or the accent falls within the word; the paper is about second-position clitics and uses accent only as a diagnostic for prosodic-word status.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect variation in tone spreading: in the Old Štokavian dialect (Zec 1993) High Tone spreads only from the final mora of a prosodic word, so an enclitic blocks spreading (dobro mi došli, p. 56); Neo-Štokavian spreads onto prepositions. The literature disagrees on whether function words such as the complementizer da are accented (Browne 1975, Magner 1991 yes; Progovac 1993, Radanović-Kocić 1988 no), and normally unaccented prepositions can carry emphatic or contrastive stress (p. 54).
new_statements.identity_note: Schütze 1994 writes about 'Serbo-Croatian' as the standard language, with side remarks on the Old Štokavian dialect (tone spreading only from a prosodic word's final mora) versus the Neo-Štokavian standard (spreading onto prepositions). Zlatić 1997 describes Serbian (Neo-Štokavian standard, with the four-way rising/falling long/short accents implicit in her 'short rising' vs 'long rising' examples). Neither describes the Zagreb or other urban stress-only varieties recorded in the existing Simonović & Kager statement.

new_statements.rule_in_words: A syntax (HPSG) dissertation with no phonology or prosody section. In passing it shows that Serbian word accent is lexically contrastive and tonal-with-length: nominalizations in -nje are distinguished by a short rising vs. a long rising accent on different vowels (process vs. result reading), and definite vs. indefinite adjectives differ by vowel length and accent pattern. No rule for accent placement is given; the rising accents named are the Neo-Štokavian ones.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; notes that clitics follow 'the first accented word (cf. Zec & Inkelas 1993) or after the first phrase' (ch5 p. 35).

sources.quote: The rising accent is a tonal span over the accented syllable (which hosts the stress) and the syllable following it. [...] Whenever there is an underlying tone hosted by a non-initial syllable, it will create a rising span over the originally tone-bearing syllable and the one preceding it (hence vòda/vOdA) and the stress will be located on the left syllable of the span. This, in combination with the general ban on final stress explains why all non-initial accents are rising (at least in native words), so that a form like *vodA is excluded. [...] the falling accents, which can occur only on the initial syllable of a word, are the underlying Hs on that syllable
sources.locator: lingbuzz preprint p. 8-9, section 4.1 (the text layer)
sources.note: OUP chapter (paywalled) but the lingbuzz preprint is open. Restates the standard generative picture: lexical H tone is contrastive; stress is predictable from tone (on the syllable before a non-initial H, on the initial syllable otherwise); falling accents only word-initial; no final stress in native words; toneless words get a default initial falling accent. Main topic is -ost nominalisations, where the 'unmarked' pattern is a rising span over a long closed penult and the final syllable.

It documents that the standard language has two prosodic implementations: the codified Neo-Štokavian pitch accent standard (tone + length + stress, verb prosody lexically distinctive) and an urban 'stress standard' (Zagreb, Rijeka, Niš..) with no tone or length, contrastive stress in nouns (ˈnovine 'newspapers' vs noˈvine 'novelties') and predictable, typically stem-final stress in verbs (poˈgled-a-ti, zaˈbol-e-ti). sources.citation: Zsiga, Elizabeth C. & Draga Zec. 2013. Contextual evidence for the representation of pitch accents in Standard Serbian. Language and Speech 56(1): 69–104. DOI 10.1177/0023830912440792. Author preprint from zsigae.com.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Instrumental (production experiment with tone crowding): 'It is proposed that both Rising and Falling accents consist of a single lexical High. The restricted distribution of the two accents emerges from the interaction of stress and tone: Falling accents are monosyllabic, such that stress and pitch prominence coincide; Rising accents are bisyllabic, such that the stressed syllable precedes the pitch-accented syllable.'
sources.note: Standard Serbian: a single lexical H per word is contrastive; stress is derived from it (syllable before a non-initial H, else initial); falling accent = H on the stressed initial syllable, rising = H on the post-tonic syllable; no final stress in polysyllables. Phonetic study confirming this representation.

sources.citation: Zec, Draga & Elizabeth C. Zsiga. 2010. Interaction of tone and stress in Standard Serbian. Formal Approaches to Slavic Linguistics 18: 536–555. Author PDF from zsigae.com.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Standard Serbian belongs to the class of hybrid prosodic systems, those that manipulate both stress and tone (Lehiste & Ivić 1986) ... two pitch accents, Falling and Rising, each defined by a characteristic pitch shape, as well as by stress, whose correlate is increase in duration.' 'The Falling PA occurs on monosyllables and the initial syllable of polysyllables, while the Rising PA occurs on all syllables of polysyllabic words other than the final.' Analysis: each word has at most one lexical H on any syllable; stress falls on the H syllable if initial, otherwise on the syllable immediately

sources.quote: BCS has four lexical pitch accents, traditionally categorized by the phonemic length of the stressed vowel and tonal alignment; they are called the short rise, short fall, long rise, and long fall (Godjevac 2000a, Smiljanic 2004). sources.note: Experimental study of focus intonation and clitic placement in Zagreb Croatian, not of lexical accent placement. Incidentally notes that Zagreb speakers neutralise the four-way pitch accent contrast (a stress variety) and that stress position is lexical there (initial in formal register, non-initial in colloquial loanwords).

sources.quote: Klaićev naglasni sustav – i opisi naglasnih sustava u starijim gramatikama hrvatskoga književnog jezika (npr. Brabec, Hraste i Živković 1970) – jasni su i, što je najvažnije, dosljedni. [...] Na jednosložnim riječima mogu stajati samo silazni naglasci. [...] Na prvom slogu višesložnih riječi može stajati bilo koji od četiriju akcenata [...] U sredini riječi – a to znači na slogu koji nije ni prvi ni zadnji – mogu stajati samo uzlazni naglasci. [...] Na zadnjem slogu u domaćim riječima ne stoji ni jedan naglasak (Brabec, Hraste i Živković 1970: 20).
sources.locator: Opačić 2014, p. 472-473 (the text layer); Vidović 2014, p. 497-498
sources.note: Book not online. Two hrcak articles on it were read. Opačić (its reviewer) says Klaić's system follows the classic Neo-Štokavian rules and restates them: monosyllables take only falling accents; the first syllable of polysyllables any of the four accents; medial syllables only rising; no accent on the final syllable of native words (English: 'On monosyllabic words only falling accents can stand.. On the first syllable of polysyllabic words any of the four accents.. In the middle of a word only rising accents.. On the last syllable of native words no accent stands'). Vidović (p. 498) adds that…
